title: PTO Bureau: Cash Advances Priced on Utility Delay
one_liner: A data co-op plus bridge lender that advances the 10-20% held back until utility Permission-to-Operate, and prices each advance from real per-utility delay history.
customer: Small and mid-size residential installers doing about 50-500 systems a year ($2-15M revenue). Their cash is squeezed post-25D. Secondary buyers are TPO sponsors and developers who need systems energized before the Dec 31, 2027 placed-in-service cliff.
problem: Lenders and TPO sponsors release most of the money at install but hold back the final 10-20% until PTO. Installer-reported PTO waits run 4-12 weeks, and about 8-12 weeks for battery systems in SCE territory. That holdback is often the entire gross margin, so an installer with 60-100 unenergized systems is one supplier-credit squeeze from insolvency. For TPO systems that did not begin construction by July 4, 2026, the 30% 48E credit requires placed-in-service by Dec 31, 2027, and tax-equity investors generally treat PTO as that trigger. Every idle week is now worth real money to sponsors.
solution: Three pieces. (1) A PTO clock: a member-contributed dataset of submit-to-PTO days by utility, AHJ, system size, and whether it includes storage, plus the recurring deficiency-notice reasons. (2) Bridge advances: buy or advance against the PTO holdback within 48 hours of a passed final inspection, priced from the clock, for example 3-6% for a system expected under 60 days. (3) PTO SWAT: a human team with utility-portal expertise that fixes and re-submits deficient interconnection packages, sold per system, and sold to sponsors as a deadline bounty for clearing backlog before the 2027 cutoff.
why_now: 25D expired Dec 31, 2025 and TPO is now the main route to a federal credit. The 48E begin-construction window closed July 4, 2026, so the 12/31/2027 placed-in-service deadline is now the binding constraint. Storm and battery-heavy interconnection queues are growing, and NEC 2026 adoption is adding deficiency notices. Traditional lenders are pulling back from small installers after the 2025-26 failures.
revenue_model: Discount fee on advances, roughly 25-40% annualized. A $150-300 per-system SWAT fee. Sponsor-paid bounties for pre-deadline energization. A later license of the PTO clock dataset to lenders, tax-equity investors and utilities.
non_obvious_insight: PTO delay looks random to outsiders but is predictable, because it comes from a few utility reviewer queues and about ten repeat deficiency reasons: single-line diagram mismatches, label errors, battery configuration and inverter list issues. Installers know their own utility's clock, but nobody has pooled it. A tiny lender that underwrites on predicted PTO days can beat big finance companies. The collateral is also better than it looks, because the system is already built and has passed the local inspection.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 installers in a single utility territory. Trade a free benchmark report for their last 12 months of PTO timestamps. Publish the resulting utility PTO clock as a lead magnet. Line up a $250-500k line from a community lender or family office. Fund the first 20 advances at installers that sell directly to a sponsor, where assignment consent is easiest. Run the SWAT service as a manual concierge for $200 per system to learn the deficiency patterns.

title: Technique Capture for Cell Therapy Tech Transfer
one_liner: Instrumented video-and-sensor capture of the 'artisanal' manual steps in cell therapy processes, turned into numeric parameters and training packages for CDMO tech transfer.
customer: Cell and gene therapy developers moving from academic or pilot scale to a CDMO, CDMO MSAT teams, and automation vendors as secondary buyers.
problem: Roughly 10% of a ~5,000-action biomanufacturing workflow is manual and resists automation, for example cell resuspension. The know-how sits in one technician's hands. As cell therapies scale and CDMOs cut staff, process know-how is getting lost in tech transfer. Failed transfers burn months and millions. Cellares' 168 layoffs after BMS ended the partnership show automation capex is fragile.
solution: A 'Technique Package': multi-angle video with hand and pose tracking, Bluetooth pipettes and force or flow sensors, timing, and cell-state images at each critical manual step. Convert it into acceptable ranges, failure signatures, operator training clips and a comparability protocol, delivered before CDMO engineering runs. With customer consent, the data doubles as a physical-AI training set.
why_now: The 5,000-action and 10% artisanal figures come from 2026 GEN reporting. CDMO staff cuts are eroding institutional knowledge. Cheap wearables and egocentric-video models are mature. Transfyr's $25M seed proves investor appetite for the underlying data but targets a different buyer.
revenue_model: $25-120k per transfer package, per-operator training licenses, and data licensing with revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: Sold as tech-transfer insurance (avoid failed engineering runs), not as automation. It needs no robot, no capex and no bet on which automation vendor survives. Buyers pay from the transfer budget, which is already allocated.
first_30_days: Build the kit from off-the-shelf parts. Offer two CGT startups planning CDMO transfers a $20-25k pilot. Capture three high-variance steps and document before-and-after run success.

title: Recurring-Gift Migration Concierge for Churches
one_liner: A fixed-fee service that moves a church's recurring donors off an expensive or hostile giving platform without losing them.
customer: Churches of 100-2,000 weekly attendees paying Pushpay, Subsplash, Tithe.ly or Ministry Brands. The buyer is the pastor, executive pastor or volunteer treasurer.
problem: Recurring gifts are the hostage. Donors' saved cards and bank accounts live inside the incumbent platform, and cancelling is punished. A Pushpay reviewer says the church is 'locked into paying $350/mo for nothing since we've migrated over to the new giving platform.' A Subsplash reviewer reports 'nearly $500 just to stop their services.' Another Subsplash reviewer, on Feb 1, 2026, says they were billed and overdrawn after trying to cancel before the 1/31 renewal. A Tithe.ly app reviewer, on Jul 2, 2026, says the company keeps debiting the account after it was closed. Another Tithe.ly reviewer says there is no way to refund a transaction sent to the wrong place.
solution: Six steps. (1) A free fee audit: upload 3 processor statements and get the effective rate, hidden monthly minimums and the card-versus-ACH mix. (2) Run the PCI-compliant card-on-file transfer to a lower-cost processor. Stripe documents this import path, which needs the old processor to release the data and can take days to weeks. (3) Run a text and email campaign that gets each donor to re-enroll in one tap when their data cannot transfer. (4) Send the cancellation notices in writing at the right time and get confirmation of no further debits. (5) Run a 90-day watch for double billing and stray debits. (6) Add ongoing recovery of failed recurring gifts.
why_now: Reviews dated 2025-2026 show AI-only support and billing disputes across the major church giving vendors. Tithe.ly reviewers cite 'an AI bot only' and a chatbot that 'freezes up'. Stripe has made bulk card-data imports a documented process, so the technical barrier is lower than it was. Year-end giving season is the peak, so churches decide in Q4 and switch in January to avoid splitting the annual giving statement year.
revenue_model: A fixed migration fee of $1,500-$4,000 per church, or 25% of the first year's verified fee savings. A $49/month giving-health add-on that retries failed recurring gifts and flags stray debits. Possible processor partner revenue, disclosed to the church.
non_obvious_insight: Churches are not stuck because the software is good. They are stuck because moving donors looks impossible, and vendors profit from that fear. The technical part is solved, since Stripe documents importing cards and ACH from a prior processor at https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/data-migrations/pan-import. What is missing is a human to run donor communications and paperwork. Evidence: Pushpay ($350/month lock-in after migrating, sales promises that differ from the contract) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/pushpay.com. Subsplash (about $500 exit penalty, overdraft after cancellation, $800 stuck 'pending') at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/subsplash.com. Tithe.ly (debits after closure, no refund path for errors) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=694740700/sortby=mostrecent/xml and https://www.trustpilot.com/review/tithe.ly. Church administrators also trade advice in denominational networks and Facebook groups, so a good migration spreads by word of mouth cheaply.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the fee-audit calculator as a spreadsheet plus a landing page, and pull the public Pushpay, Subsplash and Tithe.ly reviewers. Days 10-20: offer 20 churches the free audit through church-admin Facebook groups and denominational finance offices. Days 20-30: sign 2-3 pilot churches for a January migration and pre-sell in Q4. Confirm with a payments attorney that the transfer flow keeps the service out of PCI scope, meaning it never touches card numbers.

title: Parking-Slot Gates for Overrun Villages
one_liner: Sell tiny hotspot villages and trailheads a plate-recognition parking and coach-slot reservation system whose price rises until arrivals fit a hard cap.
customer: Municipalities, mountain and coastal park authorities and private lot operators in places like Alpine lake villages, Dolomites passes, Cinque Terre-type towns and Croatian or Greek islands. Budgets are under EUR 50K, and they already own parking revenue.
problem: Venice's day-tripper fee reportedly did not cut numbers, because a small flat fee is dwarfed by trip cost. Open villages cannot install turnstiles, but almost every day visitor arrives by car, coach or shuttle. Those arrival modes are countable and enforceable, and nobody prices them dynamically.
solution: A cheap camera and plate-recognition kit plus a web app. Visitors reserve parking and coach slots at prices that rise with demand until the cap holds. Residents and overnight guests are exempt through a plate allow-list synced from hotels' check-in data. The cap becomes a subsidy for staying overnight.
why_now: Edge computer vision and plate recognition are now cheap. Record arrivals (1.52B international in 2025) and visible failures of flat fees have made mayors ready to try hard caps. Mount Fuji's 4,000/day cap plus fee shows caps are politically acceptable, and a few Alpine lakes already require reserved road access in peak season.
revenue_model: SaaS of EUR 300-900 per month per site, plus 3-5% of slot fees collected, plus a hardware lease.
non_obvious_insight: Price the arrival mode rather than the person. Cars and coaches are the physical valve for day-trip load, and exempting overnight guests turns a congestion rule into a booking incentive that local hotels will help sell.
first_30_days: Pick 3 villages that already have paid lots. Run a manual pilot with a reservation page and a phone-camera plate check by a local attendant, with no hardware. Sign private lot operators first, since they can decide fastest. Ask mayors for a summer 2027 pilot and a letter of support.

title: Pet-Safe Demand Response With Guaranteed Temperature Floors
one_liner: A demand-response layer that ties thermostat and battery dispatch to a cheap sensor where the pet actually lives, guaranteeing a temperature floor so pet owners stop opting out of grid flexibility.
customer: Co-op and municipal utilities and VPP/DR aggregators running thermostat or battery programs, who pay per enrolled and reliably-dispatched household. Pet insurers co-fund the sensors as a heatstroke-loss and brand play.
problem: Grid flexibility is now the scarce commodity (PJM's July auction cleared at the $325/MW-day cap and came up 6.8 GW short; the Duke study found 76 GW of new load could connect with 0.25% curtailment). Thermostat DR depends on enrollment and on people not overriding events, and events land on the hottest afternoons. Roughly 95M US households own a pet, and hypothesis to test in the first month: pets are a leading reason owners opt out or override, because an animal cannot consent to 82F. Aggregators treat that as unexplained churn and lost kW.
solution: Ship a $15-25 Wi-Fi temperature/humidity sensor placed in the pet zone, integrated as a hard constraint in the dispatch engine. The engine pre-cools earlier, caps setback by heat index, and auto-releases the event if the pet-zone sensor crosses the threshold. Owners get a visible 'pet-safe' program label, and the utility gets committed kW with lower override risk. Data is shared with the insurer only with consent.
why_now: Utilities and hyperscalers are buying 'firm' distributed capacity (Sunrun/Tesla/Renew Home's 16.8 GW capacity-as-a-service, with no disclosed verification standard), and 25C/25D ended 12/31/2025, shifting the economics toward utility-paid flexibility. Summer 2026 heat and record affordability pressure make participation and reliability the bottleneck.
revenue_model: Per-enrolled-household fee from utilities/aggregators ($10-30 per household per year), pilot fees ($25-40K), insurer co-funding of sensors, and later performance bonuses tied to reduced override rates.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable DR customers are the ones who currently refuse because a living creature bears the risk. A sensor-backed guarantee converts a moral veto into a contract term, and pet insurers will subsidize it because heatstroke claims are avoidable. Verify the premise cheaply against override and opt-out data before building.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 distribution co-ops (there are hundreds) and one aggregator to add a pet-owner segment to an existing thermostat program. Survey opt-outs and pull override reasons. Hand-place 100 sensors and run one event with the pet-floor rule, comparing override rates against a control. Sell a $25-40K paid pilot with the results, and approach one pet insurer for sensor co-funding.

title: Pickleball Courts Inside Empty Fellowship Halls
one_liner: A turnkey operator that converts congregations' idle gyms and fellowship halls into revenue-sharing indoor pickleball venues, with lines, nets, insurance and booking handled.
customer: Congregations (churches, synagogues, mosques, temples) with a gym or hall and parking lot, who receive a rent share. Players (often retirees on weekday mornings) pay $8-15 per session.
problem: US pickleball grew from 13.6M (2023) to 24.3M (2025) players, but courts are scarce (about 1 dedicated court per 1,000 participants in the Mid-Atlantic, and about $900M of investment needed per a 2022 SFIA report). Outdoor courts are being restricted or closed by noise complaints. Meanwhile congregations that are shrinking or flat (only 33% of Americans attend monthly) sit on large rooms used a few hours a week, and fear liability and tax surprises.
solution: A standard hall kit (removable court lines, portable nets, wall padding, ball machine), a legal and insurance package (lease template, additional-insured wording, a flat-rent structure designed to avoid UBIT problems, waivers), a booking app with open-play scheduling and rating-linked sessions, and part-time paid hosts. Indoor play removes the neighbor-noise problem.
why_now: Participation more than doubled in two years, and noise fights are closing outdoor courts (Kirkwood MO, Walnut Creek CA, Halifax). Church rental-liability gaps are a known insurance pain point. Congregations need non-donation income.
revenue_model: Player fees of $10-14 per session. The congregation takes a 20-40% share and the operator keeps the rest less host cost. Kit rental or sale ($200/month or $3-5k) and an insurance-program commission.
non_obvious_insight: The court shortage is framed as a construction problem needing $900M. It is a liability and coordination problem: the courts already exist as 40x70 ft hardwood rooms with parking, owned by institutions that want steady income but cannot underwrite risk. A congregation is also a more trusted neighbor than a new commercial club.
first_30_days: Sign 3 congregations with gyms in one metro through denominational property committees and local pickleball Facebook groups. Run two open-play nights a week using a $1.5k kit. Pre-sell via local groups, track fill rate, and get a church-insurer quote. Aim for $1-2k revenue in the first month.

title: Savings Groups as Verified Human Endpoints for Agents
one_liner: A group-guaranteed 'verify this physical fact' API, fulfilled by African savings groups and starting with solar and battery installations.
customer: Donor-funded energy-access results-based-financing programme administrators (who pay per verified installation), inverter and battery brands verifying warranties and distributor claims, and asset lenders and insurers. Agents that need physical facts are the long-term buyer.
problem: Agents can hire humans, but RentAHuman had about 590,000 sign-ups against about 11,300 active bounties and 5,500 completed jobs, plus scams and payment errors. Trusted agent demand is scarce because individual anonymous workers are a bad trust unit. Meanwhile Africa's distributed solar and battery boom (about 17 GW in 2026) is largely invisible: Ember's estimates are about 2x official statistics, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Lenders, insurers and utilities cannot verify what exists.
solution: A verify(system, location) API exposed as an MCP tool and payable by x402 or MPP. Fulfillment goes to savings groups (VSLAs and farmer groups), which already have joint-liability norms and a treasurer. Members capture device-attested photos, inverter-app screenshots, kWh readings and GPS. Random cross-checks by other members catch fraud, and a small bond from pooled savings backs each group. Payment goes to the group's mobile-money account, not to anonymous individuals.
why_now: The Hormuz energy shock and the solar and battery boom are pulling in subsidy programmes and lenders who need verification. Sandi AI shows 10,000+ farmer groups are already digitized in Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. The public failure of agent-hiring marketplaces has created demand for a trust layer. Machine-payment protocols make per-task settlement cheap.
revenue_model: $4-8 per verification: about 65% to the group, 10% to the bond pool, 25% platform margin. Later, recurring data subscriptions on verified asset registries.
non_obvious_insight: Individuals are the wrong unit of trust for agent-issued work. A group with existing joint liability solves identity, fraud, payout and dispute in one move. Demand-first beats marketplace-first: RBF programmes already pay for verification today, so agents can be layered on afterwards.
first_30_days: Partner with an existing savings-group network (for example Sandi AI or a VSLA association) and onboard 20 groups in Uganda. Pitch one RBF administrator or battery distributor a 500-check pilot at $6 each. Run the verification workflow on WhatsApp and mobile money, with manual review of every submission.

title: Bale Grade Audits With Premium Sharing
one_liner: Independent PET and HDPE bale audits, plus MRF line tuning paid from the price uplift, to turn 'commodity bales' into measured, spec-priced material.
customer: Independent MRFs selling plastic bales (pay a share of uplift) and the surviving US reclaimers, who pay for supplier scoring and dispute referee services.
problem: Feedstock PET bales hit 1.44 cents/lb in April 2026 and seven of about 30 US reclaimers closed. Yet New Jersey delayed its food-contact PCR mandate citing constrained food-grade supply, while recyclers say HDPE blow-mold supply is 'not constrained.' That points to a quality-tier mismatch, not a shortage.
solution: Third-party bale audits (manual composition sort, handheld NIR, moisture and weight) that produce a bale spec sheet. A tuning playbook for optical-sorter recipes and QC pickers. Contracts that pay MRFs on measured tier and give reclaimers a lot-level dispute referee.
why_now: The 2026 price collapse and reclaimer closures leave the remaining buyers desperate for predictable quality. The mandate delays mean brands cannot lock supply, so spec-priced material becomes the negotiating currency.
revenue_model: $150-400 per audited load, plus 25-35% of documented price uplift for 6-12 months, plus an annual supplier-scoring subscription for reclaimers.
non_obvious_insight: The 'shortage' insiders cite is a shortage of known-quality material. A measured bale is a different commodity, and no third party captures the gap between 1.44 cents and reclaimer-grade pricing because no one measures it.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 independent MRFs and 1 reclaimer. Manually audit 30 bales and publish the anonymized quality spread. Offer a 6-month uplift-share deal. Buy or borrow a handheld NIR ($10-25K) and standardize the photo protocol.

title: AI-Use Attestation to Keep SMB Liability Cover
one_liner: As liability policies exclude generative AI, small firms need underwriter-ready proof of AI controls to win affirmative cover, and independent agencies need a renewal ritual that keeps them relevant.
customer: Independent insurance agencies (about 37k remain) that place GL and E&O for law firms, accountants, marketing agencies, clinics and contractors, plus those SMB clients.
problem: ISO's gen-AI exclusion is already on thousands of CGL policies (Insurance Business, 2026-09-16). AI-specialist insurers target tech firms, not a dental practice using an AI receptionist. Agencies can't advise and carriers haven't said what evidence they'd accept, so clients discover the gap at claim time.
solution: A lightweight AI Use Register: discover which AI tools staff use (SSO and browser discovery), apply policy templates and human-review logging, and output a standardized attestation that a panel of MGAs and carriers agree to accept for endorsements or premium credits. Agencies white-label it into their renewal workflow.
why_now: Exclusions are spreading now, independent agencies are shrinking (39k in 2024 to 37k in 2026, Insurance Journal) yet still sell 95% of commercial insurance through humans, and insurtech's dollars (99.1% of Q2 funding is AI-centric) go to back-office tools, not SMB risk evidence.
revenue_model: $49-$149 per month per SMB, billed via the agency or the client, plus MGA per-policy referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Carriers don't yet know what evidence they want, so whoever standardizes the artifact defines it, as cyber questionnaires and scans did for Coalition and At-Bay. Agencies get a reason to call every client at renewal.
first_30_days: Interview five underwriters on what evidence they'd accept. Ship a spreadsheet-and-form v0 of the register. Sell it to 10 agencies through state agent-association chapters and get 30 SMBs onto paid plans.

title: Medicaid Look-Back Packet Builder
one_liner: Turn 60 months of messy bank statements into a caseworker-ready Medicaid application packet with explanations, so families avoid 'failure to provide verification' denials.
customer: Adult children and POA agents applying for nursing-home Medicaid for a parent ($299-$499 per case), plus elder-law and Medicaid-planning firms and senior placement advisors ($500-$1,500/month seats or per-case fees).
problem: Long-term-care Medicaid reviews up to 60 months of statements for every open account and every account closed within the window. Caseworkers typically demand written explanations for each expenditure over about $500. If records are missing the application is likely denied for 'failure to provide verification'. POA agents often lack online access to old or closed accounts, and banks can charge research fees for paper copies. Meanwhile the parent's care bills accumulate and elder-law attorneys charge thousands.
solution: Upload statements (PDF, CSV or bank link) and use OCR and an LLM to build the ledger. Detect large transfers, gifts, transfers to relatives and round-number withdrawals. Show likely penalty-period exposure. Draft the explanation letters and a caseworker index with state-specific checklists. Auto-generate missing-statement request letters to banks with a POA cover page, track which accounts are still missing, and hand the attorney a clean exception report. A separate 'consolidate and simplify before you need Medicaid' mode targets families planning ahead.
why_now: Document extraction and bank-data aggregation now make a 60-month review a minutes-long task rather than paralegal hours. Federal law (H.R. 1) sets a $1M Medicaid home-equity cap from Jan 1, 2028, and the 2026 baseline is $752,000 in most states, so more middle-class families in expensive housing markets will need spend-down or planning. State caseworkers will also be stretched by the 2027 work-requirement rollout, making complete first-time packets more valuable.
revenue_model: $299-$499 per family packet, $99 'look-back risk scan' as a lead magnet, and $500-$1,500/month firm seats or $75-$150 per case for elder-law offices, with placement-advisor referral fees as a secondary channel.
non_obvious_insight: The denial reason is paperwork, not eligibility: the requirement to explain each $500+ transaction and produce statements for closed accounts is a software-shaped burden that elder-law attorneys currently bill by the hour. See the documentation rules and 'likely deny for failure to provide verification' language at https://www.paelderlaw.net/medicaid-application-process-5-year-look-back-5-years-of-records-for-small-and-inactive-accounts/. The home-equity change is at https://justiceinaging.org/hr1-imposes-new-limit-on-home-equity-for-medicaid-ltss-effective-2028/. Bank refusal to deal with POA agents compounds it (https://www.aarp.org/caregiving/financial-legal/power-of-attorney-bank-approval/). Reddit was unreachable, so this rests on legal-practice and AARP sources describing the recurring r/AgingParents 'Mom needs Medicaid, what do they want?' situation.
first_30_days: Start with one state with clear caseworker checklists (Pennsylvania or New York). Hand-build 5 packets for free for local elder-law paralegals to validate the exception logic, then productize statement parsing and letter generation. Sell a $99 risk scan and a $349 packet through caregiver Facebook groups and 3-5 elder-law and placement-advisor partners, aiming for 10 paid packets and one firm pilot.

title: Used-Satellite Exchange With Independent Health Reports
one_liner: A broker and due-diligence shop that turns dead or distressed operators' on-orbit assets into sellable, verified inventory.
customer: Buyers: acquirers of the Rocket Lab type, infrastructure and PE funds, and governments or startups that want a quick constellation. Sellers: bankruptcy trustees, venture-debt lenders, insurers and cash-strapped first-generation smallsat operators.
problem: Insiders assume a satellite is worthless when its company dies. But the bus, license, orbit and customer contracts can still hold value, and buyers cannot verify condition. Lenders have no repossession or title process, and every M&A team improvises technical diligence.
solution: Two products. (1) An independent 'fleet health report' built from open orbital data (maneuver history, decay, propulsion-use proxies, beacon and telemetry checks) plus data-room review. (2) A brokerage that matches on-orbit assets and licenses to buyers, with regulator-approved license transfers handled by counsel.
why_now: Rocket Lab's roughly $8B Iridium deal and its CFO's 'more M&A' comment show on-orbit assets are being priced. 4,517 satellites deployed in 2025 means a large aging first-generation cohort. Funding is bifurcating into nine-figure rounds for a few winners and starvation for the rest.
revenue_model: $25-100k per health report. 3-8% success fee on brokered deals. Annual subscription for lenders and insurers who want portfolio monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: In space, value sits in the license, the orbit and the operating bus, and none of the three dies with the company. The missing piece is trusted third-party verification, which is a service business rather than a rocket business.
first_30_days: Publish free health scorecards on 20 public constellations to build credibility. Interview five venture-debt lenders and two space insurers about their current diligence. Sell two paid reports to funds looking at consolidation targets. Ask trustees of failed smallsat companies to list assets with you.

title: Memory Safe-Harbor: Stop Shredding Server DRAM
one_liner: A component-level sanitization policy plus a resale desk that lets neoclouds and enterprises reuse retired DRAM, CPUs and GPUs instead of shredding whole servers.
customer: Neoclouds, colocation operators, banks and healthcare IT asset managers refreshing servers, with ITADs as the channel. They pay a fixed fee and take a resale share.
problem: Data-center hardware turns over in 12-18 months and a GPU server rack can exceed $1M. DRAM is up about 400% since early 2024. Many enterprise policies still shred whole servers, destroying volatile memory that holds no persistent data. One client reportedly gained 'eight figures' just by pre-triaging refurbish versus scrap.
solution: Publish and audit a per-server-model matrix of which components persist data (SSDs, NVDIMMs, BMC and NIC flash, TPMs) and which do not (DIMMs, most compute and mechanical parts). Get it signed off by a security auditor and the client's CISO. Then run the part-out desk. Data-bearing parts are wiped or destroyed with serialized custody. Everything else is graded, tested and sold to secondary buyers.
why_now: The 2025-26 memory price spike turns shredding into a cash-burning act. AI capex has created huge, fast-cycling retiring fleets, and Sumitomo's GreenTek acquisition shows ITAD is being bought as a trading business.
revenue_model: 40-60% resale share to the client after costs, a $10-30K policy and audit fee per client, and a per-serial chain-of-custody fee.
non_obvious_insight: 'Shred everything' is a compliance habit, not a security requirement. The barrier is organizational sign-off, not technology. Whoever ships a pre-approved risk framework gets inventory that no one else can touch.
first_30_days: Write a 10-page component sanitization matrix for the 5 most common GPU and CPU server models. Have a security-audit firm review it. Pitch 10 neocloud and colo IT asset leads and 5 mid-size ITADs. Run a one-rack pilot on revenue share.

title: Savings Groups Finance Apprenticeships via Income-Share
one_liner: A mobile-money tool that lets a village savings group use its year-end share-out to pay a workshop for a young member's apprenticeship and starter toolkit, then collect 10-12% of that apprentice's income for two years back into the group.
customer: Village savings and loan groups, chamas and small SACCOs of 20-30 members in Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania, which pay the fees. Workshops and TVET trainers who get paid upfront, and employers such as solar installers who want certified graduates, pay referral and placement fees.
problem: Formal training plus tools costs $150-500, which is out of reach for a household living on irregular farm income. Youth have no credit history. Income-share agreements have mostly failed in rich countries because income verification and collection cost more than the loan. Meanwhile savings groups hold a pile of cash at each year-end share-out and have few productive places to put it.
solution: A USSD and WhatsApp workflow. The group votes on a candidate. The group pays the trainer in tranches confirmed by attendance and milestone photos. The tool collects a set share of the graduate's mobile-money income into the group ledger, and members receive returns pro rata. Social collateral does the enforcement, so no bureau or aggregator is needed. Legally it is structured as an income-linked group loan, not a security.
why_now: Sandi AI reports 10,000+ farmer groups across Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania pooling savings for solar irrigation instead of borrowing, so groups will invest pooled money in productive assets. Africa's solar and battery installs are growing about 45% a year and 75% of that is distributed, which creates paid technician work. With six seed rounds for every Series A, outside capital is scarce and group capital is the reachable pool. Reported pressure on Gulf remittances, about $50bn at risk, weakens family-funded schooling.
revenue_model: A 4% origination fee on training payments, 1% of repayments, and 5-8% referral fees from trainers and tool vendors. Placement fees of about $20 per graduate come from installers and employers. Youth-employment funders can pay $100-200 per verified income outcome, which is what makes the thin margin work at small scale.
non_obvious_insight: The income-share agreement broke in rich countries on enforcement, and a savings group solves enforcement at zero marginal cost because members know the apprentice, the workshop and the family. The year-end share-out also lands in December, right before January apprenticeship intake, so a timing mismatch becomes a built-in cash cycle.
first_30_days: Partner with a savings-group promoter NGO or a platform like Sandi AI. Choose five groups within three months of their share-out. Sign three workshops (welding, solar installation, motorcycle repair or tailoring) to milestone-based payment. Launch 10 apprenticeships worth $3-4k, funded by the groups' own money plus a small first-loss guarantee from a grant. Track progress by photo and voice notes on WhatsApp, and record the first income repayments.

title: Phishing Simulations for Agent Approvers
one_liner: Plant known-bad agent actions into human approval queues and prove to auditors and insurers that your reviewers actually catch them.
customer: Heads of finance ops, claims, compliance and internal audit at companies whose agents require human approval (payments, refunds, claims, access requests, code merges), plus cyber underwriters who ask about controls.
problem: Human-in-the-loop is the default answer to agent risk. Step two: volume makes approval a reflex, so the gate decays into a rubber stamp. Step three: regulators and auditors ask for oversight that is demonstrable and measurable (EU AI Act Article 14 and NIST AI RMF language), and no company can show that reviewers catch anything. Injected test cases are recommended in practice writing, but nobody productizes them.
solution: Middleware in the approval path (Slack, Teams, ServiceNow or custom queues) that injects synthetic, internally labeled bad cases at calibrated rates: a vendor bank-detail change, an out-of-policy refund, a prompt-injected request. It measures catch rate and latency by reviewer, queue and time of day, and adapts injection frequency. Output is an oversight effectiveness report with confidence intervals for auditors and insurers, plus queue-design advice (fewer, better gates).
why_now: Agents multiply approval volume. The EU AI Act's human-oversight requirements are still on the books for 2027 and insurers now ask about controls in questionnaires. Approval fatigue is widely acknowledged but unmeasured.
revenue_model: $2-8k/month per approval workflow, or $30-$100k/year enterprise licenses, with an audit-evidence add-on.
non_obvious_insight: KnowBe4 built a large company by testing humans rather than training them. The presence of a reviewer is not a control, but a measured catch rate is, and it doubles as evidence in insurance and audit conversations.
first_30_days: Build for Slack approvals with an accounts-payable bank-change scenario. Run it with 3 finance-ops teams and deliver a first report stating how many planted errors reviewers caught. Use anonymized catch-rate results as the sales asset.

title: Sponsor-Paid Care Network for Canine Trials
one_liner: Biotechs pay for dogs' cancer care in exchange for clean, immune-competent efficacy data, solving pet-owner affordability and drug-developer validation at once.
customer: Clinical-stage biotechs (including AI-drug-discovery companies) and animal-health developers that need cheap in vivo efficacy and safety signals pay per enrolled dog. General-practice and specialty clinics are site partners. Foundations can co-fund.
problem: 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never receive IV chemo. On the other side, AI-designed drugs are bottlenecked by assays and validation, mouse models predict poorly, and FDA's Sept 21, 2026 rule makes sponsors show that non-animal methods are 'adequately validated'. Spontaneous tumors in pet dogs (lymphoma, osteosarcoma, mast cell, bladder cancer) are well-established human-relevant models, yet trials struggle to recruit because the dogs are first seen in general practices.
solution: A network of 30-60 general practices plus a few specialty centers. AI trial-matching runs over practice-management data and an owner-facing trial finder. Sponsors fund a standard-of-care baseline (diagnostics and supportive care) so owners get treatment free. The studio handles owner consent, GCP-style data capture, INAD/CVM paperwork, and opt-in blood and tissue banking. Start with observational registries and PK/PD window studies of oral and repurposed generic drugs, then move to sponsor-funded interventional studies.
why_now: AI-biotech funding is over $6B in 2026 and sponsors are hunting for validation evidence. FDA's Sept 2026 rule and its 25-use-case NAM database push developers away from lab animals without banning them. Duffield ($250M) and PetSmart Charities are funding 'access to care', so grant co-funding for clinics is available. Oral options like Laverdia now make community-level oncology treatable.
revenue_model: $15-30k per enrolled dog (treatment, site fees, monitoring, data), at roughly 30% gross margin. $100-250k per observational registry or PK window study. Foundation grants subsidize owner-side costs.
non_obvious_insight: Pet trials fail on recruitment and owner cost, not on science. The general-practice vet is where 90% of cases first appear, and no one connects them to sponsors. Turning a sponsor's development budget into owners' treatment budgets solves the affordability crisis and delivers a data product for drug developers.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 clinics and one board-certified oncologist as scientific lead. Pitch 10 biotechs on a $100-200k canine lymphoma real-world-outcomes registry or a dog PK window study of a repurposed oral drug. Co-apply for a foundation grant to cover owner costs. Keep the first studies observational or extra-label to stay clear of the heavier INAD requirements. First revenue in about 4-6 months.

title: SNAP-Ready Kits for Corner Stores
one_liner: A UPC-level 'variety counter' plus a pre-built wholesale fill kit that tells a convenience store exactly what to stock to keep SNAP authorization under USDA's new staple-food rule.
customer: Independent convenience stores, bodegas, small groceries and dollar-format stores that accept SNAP (USDA counts 269,217 authorized retailers, with small-format stores hit hardest). The store owner pays for the audit and kit. Secondary payers are the local cash-and-carry wholesalers and jobbers who earn incremental case sales, and city or state health departments that fund healthy-corner-store programs.
problem: USDA's final rule (effective July 7, 2026; implementation Nov 4, 2026) raises the stocking floor from 3 to 7 varieties in each of 4 staple categories (28 varieties), with 3 stocking units each (84 units) and perishables in 3 categories. The counting rules are counterintuitive: brown and white rice are one variety, all bread is one variety, and brands and flavors do not count. USDA's own analysis of 121,294 small-format stores found only 52% already stock enough dairy varieties and 63% enough protein, which implies roughly 58,000 stores short on dairy alone. Stores are assessed at reauthorization (every 5 years, about 54,000 stores a year) or at any time. Owners have no tool that tells them what to buy, and commenters said the rule is infeasible for small stores.
solution: An SMS and web tool. The owner uploads a POS export or photographs shelves. A classifier maps UPCs to USDA's variety groups, using the rule's Group 1 and Group 2 counting logic, and returns a gap list such as 'need 3 more dairy varieties and 2 more protein varieties, buy these SKUs'. A sold-through kit pre-negotiated with a local wholesaler uses the lowest-spoilage items that fit small refrigeration. The tool also produces a USDA evidence pack (dated photos, invoices, variety ledger) for reauthorization or a compliance review. A 'keep or drop SNAP' ROI calculator is built in, because most small stores earn little from SNAP.
why_now: USDA published the final rule on May 8, 2026 and the enforcement-ready implementation date is Nov 4, 2026, about five weeks out. The prior interim standard was only 3 varieties per category, so almost every small store has a gap to close. USDA also says it can assess any retailer at any time, and every store hits reauthorization within 5 years, so demand arrives as a rolling wave rather than a single date.
revenue_model: $79 one-time shelf audit, or free through wholesaler partners. Kit sold at wholesale plus a 10-15% margin, or a referral fee from the wholesaler. $29 per month monitoring with auto-reorder and evidence-pack refresh. Grant-funded 100-store packages ($500-1,500 per store) sold to health departments and food-access nonprofits. Anonymized gap data licensed to distributors.
non_obvious_insight: USDA admits it has no baseline data on how many stores fail, and its roughly $77M first-year cost estimate describes 'reviewing notice, guidance, and updating stock', which works out to a few hundred dollars per store. That looks far too low against stocking 28 varieties with perishables in tiny coolers, and commenters said so directly: 'refrigerated space is limited for perishable products... would lead to waste and higher operating costs' and 'stocking seven distinct grain varieties... is not feasible for small convenience stores'. Convenience stores are 44% of SNAP retailers but only 5% of redemptions and 76% of sanctions, so many owners will do the math and drop SNAP unless compliance is cheap and certain. The rule also leaves 'perishable' and 'stocking unit' undefined, which creates an interpretation gap that a shared variety ledger can fill. Evidence: final rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/08/2026-09137/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance and proposed rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/09/25/2025-18624/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance
first_30_days: Pick one metro with dense small-format stores. Sign one cash-and-carry wholesaler or jobber as the kit supplier. Encode the rule's variety-counting logic into a spreadsheet-based counter and walk 40 stores with a $79 audit, aiming for 15 paid audits and 5 kit orders. Publish a one-page 'what counts as a variety' guide and post it in grocer association WhatsApp and Facebook groups. Pitch the local health department a grant-funded 100-store pilot using the audit results as proof.

title: Extranet Takeover Defense for Independent Hotels
one_liner: Managed monitoring and fraud response for hotels' OTA extranet logins and guest-messaging channels, the credential theft that turns into guest payment scams.
customer: Independent hotels, B&Bs and small STR managers of 10-150 rooms, their channel-manager and PMS resellers, and cyber insurers.
problem: Attackers phish or infect front-desk staff, take over OTA extranet accounts and message arriving guests from the genuine booking thread asking for payment via fraudulent links. The hotel absorbs chargebacks and reputational damage and can lose OTA account standing. These hotels have no IT staff and are too small for security vendors.
solution: A light service that watches for leaked credentials tied to the hotel's domain and staff emails, alerts on suspicious extranet login emails, flags guest messages containing external links or payment requests, and runs 10-minute staff phishing training. It adds a 24/7 hotline for incident response and a guest-facing 'how we ask for payment' page.
why_now: AI-written phishing in dozens of languages, widely reported hospitality-targeted credential theft campaigns in 2025, and merchant-model payments that concentrate risk in OTA accounts. Insurers are hardening cyber requirements.
revenue_model: EUR 49-149 per property per month, insurer commissions and per-incident response fees.
non_obvious_insight: The weak node is the hotel's front-desk laptop, not the OTA platform. The unit of attack is a booking thread the guest already trusts, so simple detection at the message level gives most of the protection.
first_30_days: Run a free credential-exposure scan for 100 hotel domains using public breach data. Send each hotel its results, convert 10 to paid, and partner with two hotel associations for distribution.

title: IEP-Ready Adaptive Hardware, Printed to Order
one_liner: A micro-manufacturer that acts as the approved vendor for special-education adaptive hardware, starting with custom AAC keyguards for tablets and expanding to OT-prescribed grips, switch mounts and positioning aids.
customer: School district special-ed and assistive-technology coordinators, school SLPs and OTs, and private pediatric therapy clinics, paid through district purchase orders funded by IEP obligations.
problem: Free keyguard designs exist, and Etsy sellers make standard ones. But an SLP has no time to print, a district can't pay an Etsy seller by purchase order, and a custom AAC grid on a specific tablet and case needs an exact fit. Legally required AT then arrives weeks late. Every tablet or case refresh orphans last year's keyguards.
solution: A catalog and a 48-hour custom service. The SLP uploads a screenshot of the AAC layout and the tablet and case model. We return a fit-verified keyguard with an IEP-friendly quote and invoice. Then expand to OT-prescribed items (pencil grips, adaptive handles, switch and tablet mounts, tactile schedule boards) using a clinician-approved parametric library. Paperwork arrives ready for the file: W-9, liability insurance, net-30 terms and cooperative-purchasing listings.
why_now: Consumer-grade printing is now reliable enough for small runs of durable parts. Tablet-based AAC is now standard practice, and app grid layouts are standardized enough to parametrize. Districts are under pressure to meet AT obligations with tight budgets. Open-source designs prove the demand but leave the procurement gap wide open.
revenue_model: Per item ($35 to $95 for keyguards; $10 to $150 for other adaptive items), plus an annual district 'AT Bench' subscription ($3k to $8k covering a set number of custom items and a design consult).
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing isn't the printing or even the design, since clinicians will share designs for free. It's the procurement wrapper: being a vendor a district can legally and easily pay. Whoever holds 'approved vendor' status with a few purchasing cooperatives gets pulled into every district's AT budget. Print cost is $4 against a $80 to $150 price because the customer is paying for zero-friction compliance and clinical fit.
first_30_days: Take the open-source keyguard parametric files and verify fit against the five most common tablet and case combinations. Post in SLP and AT groups: 'send a screenshot of your layout, first keyguard at cost, PO accepted.' Complete vendor registration with two districts and apply to one purchasing cooperative. Target 15 paid orders and one district relationship.

title: Contingency-Fee 45F Childcare Tax Credit Shop
one_liner: An R&D-credit-style boutique that finds, structures and files the newly expanded employer childcare credit (40%, or 50% for small businesses, capped at $500k/$600k) for firms already spending on childcare.
customer: Mid-market employers (200-5,000 staff) with onsite care or vendor childcare spend: hospitals, manufacturers, universities, credit unions and restaurant chains. Referral channel: their CPA firms.
problem: The 45F credit was rarely used under its old cap. From January 1, 2026 the credit rose to 40% (50% small business) with $500k ($600k) caps. Eligibility turns on contract structure, licensing, enrollment open to employees and documentation, and it interacts with the new $7,500 DCFSA limit. Generalist CPAs don't know it and CFOs have never claimed it.
solution: A two-week diagnostic reviews contracts and spend, restructures where needed (for example, reserved-slot agreements with licensed local centers or consortium models), computes the credit and files the forms alongside the client's CPA. Reserved-slot deals also give centers guaranteed enrollment, which helps supply.
why_now: The changes took effect January 2026, employers set 2027 benefit budgets in Q4 2026, and the first full filing season under the new rules is early 2027.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 15-20% of credit claimed (a $250k credit yields $40-50k). Add-on brokerage fee for slot-reservation contracts.
non_obvious_insight: A $500k cap means the credit can fund a whole classroom's worth of care per employer. The constraint is know-how, not money, and reserved-slot contracts turn a tax credit into childcare supply, a desert fix hidden in the tax code.
first_30_days: Partner with a tax attorney or CPA who has done R&D or WOTC credits. Build a list of 200 employers advertising childcare benefits (job posts, hospital filings). Publish a two-page 45F guide and a free eligibility screen. Aim for 3 signed contingency engagements.

title: Escaped-Burn Liability Cover Verified From Orbit
one_liner: Go/no-go data and liability cover for prescribed burn associations, priced from fuel dryness and settled by satellite proof that the fire never left the unit.
customer: Prescribed burn associations, contract burn bosses and private landowners (ranchers, forest owners) in Texas, Oklahoma, the Great Plains, the Southeast, Colorado and the West Coast. Surplus-lines MGAs, insurers and state forestry agencies are the second customer.
problem: Prescribed fire is the cheapest wildfire-adaptation tool, but escaped-fire liability cover is described as 'unavailable, unaffordable and vital' in places like Oregon and Colorado. Only a few risk pools exist, such as three Georgia burn associations with about 1,600 members. Insurers cannot price it because after an escape nobody has objective evidence of what was burned or when.
solution: Phase 1 is a software and certificate business that needs no insurance licence. A per-burn pack combines satellite live fuel-moisture and soil-dryness signals with forecasts as a documented go/no-go. A 72-hour containment certificate compares thermal hotspots (VIIRS, FireSat, commercial thermal) and next-day burn-scar perimeter (Sentinel-2 and Landsat at 10-30 m) against the permitted unit. Phase 2 has a partner MGA or risk retention group underwrite association pools, with verification making claims close to binary.
why_now: FireSat's first three operational satellites (July 2026) will deliver at least twice-daily data to early adopters by end-2026, heading to about 20 satellites and hourly revisit by 2029. Suppression backlogs and insurance retreat are pushing states to legalise more burning, and the Nov-Apr burn season starts within weeks. New free 10-30 m optical and radar archives make unit-level perimeter checks nearly free to produce.
revenue_model: $95-$250 per burn certificate plus $1.50-$3 per acre. Association memberships of $1-3K/yr. Later, MGA commission or a data licence to insurers underwriting pools.
non_obvious_insight: Prescribed fire is uninsurable not because it is risky but because nobody can prove afterwards that it stayed inside the line. An objective, cheap orbital perimeter check turns an unpriceable moral-hazard argument into an auditable event. Gross-negligence liability standards in state burn laws turn on documented preparation, which the go/no-go pack supplies.
first_30_days: Offer free winter-season pilots to 10 burn associations (TX, OK, NE, GA, CO) and build the containment check on free VIIRS, Sentinel-2 and Landsat data while applying for FireSat early-adopter access. Start charging $95 per certificate from December. Get one surplus-lines broker or MGA to review the certificate format as the seed of a Phase 2 pool.

title: Pattern-Less Foundry Network via Printed Sand Molds
one_liner: Print sand molds centrally and pour them at idle small foundries to deliver castings in about two weeks with no patterns.
customer: Pump, valve, ag-equipment and machinery OEMs and repair shops needing 5-500 castings. Small foundries are the supply side.
problem: Small-lot castings from Asia now face tariffs and freight up to 50% higher. Domestic foundries quote long lead times, largely because of pattern-making and minimum runs, and aging owners are retiring or closing. Castings are an invisible bottleneck under reshoring and under Section 232 derivative rates.
solution: A hub with binder-jet sand printing (or rented capacity at existing bureaus) prints mold and core packages from customer CAD plus solidification simulation. Ship them to 10-30 small foundries that pour iron, steel or aluminum. The network handles NDT, dimensional checks and certs, including melt origin. Start with one or two alloys and repair and replacement parts.
why_now: Printed sand has improved in cost and speed, tariffs and freight punish imported castings, foundries are consolidating, and simulation and AI gating design are cheap.
revenue_model: Per-casting pricing with 25-35% gross margin. $500-3k engineering fee per part. Foundries pay for mold volume routed to them.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is patterns and scheduling, not melting. Many small foundries have idle furnace hours but no digital front door, and a printed mold is a universal interface. US-melt certification is a sales kicker, not the core.
first_30_days: Sign three foundries with idle capacity. Buy printed molds from an existing bureau. Take 10 orders for obsolete pump or gearbox housings at $1-3k each, using 3D scans of broken parts.

title: Independent Robot Bake-Off and Acceptance Lab
one_liner: A neutral test cell where warehouse buyers watch robots handle their own SKUs and pallets before signing, with published, verified throughput numbers.
customer: Mid-size 3PLs, grocers and retailers (roughly 50-500k sq ft) evaluating palletizing, picking or humanoid pilots. Robot vendors are a second payer (for certification), and lenders and insurers are a third.
problem: Vendors control the demo. Buyers cannot verify throughput on their own product mix, and pilots eat 6-12 months. Funding is running far ahead of proof: Maven raised a $100M Series A with about 8 robots deployed, Agility booked $1.8M of revenue against a $2.5B SPAC valuation, and early 1X NEO demos were largely teleoperated.
solution: Rent a 20-30k sq ft cell in a logistics hub. Buyers ship 200 pallets or 500 SKUs. Vendors run their robots under a standard protocol. The lab logs picks per hour, error rate, human-intervention minutes, teleop minutes and mean time between failures, then issues a 'Verified Throughput' report. Buyers pay per bake-off, and vendors pay to list certified results and retest after software updates.
why_now: In 2026 procurement teams face a flood of unverifiable claims: about 22k humanoids shipped in H1, nine-figure rounds go to companies with a handful of deployed units, and buyers want outcome pricing. Nobody independent sits between vendors and buyers.
revenue_model: $15-40k per buyer-commissioned bake-off, $25-75k a year per vendor for certification and retests, and data licensing of failure-mode datasets to insurers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The industry's binding constraint is trust in claims, not capability. Vendors will pay for independent verification because their real bottleneck is a 9-12 month sales cycle (compare UL, J.D. Power, Wirecutter). The failure-mode data becomes an asset that insurers, lenders and model developers all want.
first_30_days: Rent demo floor space inside a friendly integrator's or 3PL's idle mezzanine. Sign 2 mid-size 3PLs to paid bake-offs of 3 vendors each, and give vendors a free first test in exchange for the right to publish. Release the public methodology and a first leaderboard of 'intervention minutes per hour'.

title: Insurability Passport Attached to California Home Listings
one_liner: A pre-listing report that verifies wildfire mitigation and attaches bindable insurance options (FAIR Plan plus wraparound, admitted where available) to the listing, so buyers see the real insured cost before they make an offer.
customer: Listing agents and sellers in California wildfire-exposed ZIP codes, paying $149-299 per listing. MGAs and agencies pay commissions on policies that bind from the passport.
problem: Buyers, lenders and agents cannot tell before contract whether a house can be insured or at what price. The FAIR Plan grew to 696,562 policies and $768B of exposure by June 2026 (up 157% since September 2022). Seven of California's twelve largest insurers have stopped writing new business or renewing. Deals slip or die when insurance is discovered in escrow.
solution: A listing add-on that combines a mitigation inspection (Zone 0, vents, roof, photos), an insurability status by carrier type, and indicative premiums for FAIR Plan plus a difference-in-conditions wrap, and admitted quotes where they exist. It also identifies the cheapest mitigation actions that would change eligibility or price. The seller shows a QR code on the listing, and buyers can bind from the passport.
why_now: The California Department of Insurance is pushing the FAIR Plan to offer broader comprehensive coverage (Make It FAIR Act, AB 1680, announced 2026-02-02). Liberty Mutual and Safeco began nonrenewing California condo and renter policies from 2026-01-01. The state also mandates wildfire safety discounts for verified mitigation.
revenue_model: Listing fee of $149-299 for the passport. Commission on bound policies through a partner agency or MGA (typically 10-15% of premium). Optional referral fees from mitigation contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Insurance availability is being handled after the offer, in escrow, although it decides affordability at the moment of offer. Evidence: the FAIR Plan's own key statistics page shows 696,562 policies, $768B exposure and 'fewer coverage options available' in the voluntary market (https://www.cfpnet.com/key-statistics-data/). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_FAIR_Plan lists seven of twelve top insurers pausing new business or renewals. https://www.claimsjournal.com/news/west/2024/12/20/328011.htm shows Safeco and Liberty Mutual leaving condo and renters lines, with nonrenewals beginning 2026-01-01. https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2026/release005-2026.cfm describes the pending FAIR Plan coverage overhaul. Pre-listing home inspections became a normal seller expense; an insurability passport is the next one, and the mitigation data feeds the moratorium idea above. The main risk is that carrier and FAIR Plan quoting cannot be automated quickly, so start with manual agent-assisted quotes.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 listing agents in Altadena, Sierra Madre, Santa Rosa and Bay Area WUI markets. Partner with one independent agency that quotes FAIR Plan plus DIC. Build a one-page passport (photos, mitigation checklist, three quote scenarios) and deliver it manually for 10 listings at a launch price of $99. Track how many escrows it saves and use those cases to raise the price.

title: Teleoperated Pack-and-Pick Robots Piloted from Latin America
one_liner: Robot arms run by foundation models, with remote pilots in Guatemala or Colombia fixing the edge cases, sold per box.
customer: Berry, tomato and cucumber packhouses and greenhouses that lost crews.
problem: Farm labor shrank by at least 155,000 and crews were lost in 2026 harvests, while robots pick at 50-60% of human speed and fail on edge cases.
solution: Rent arms with a vision-language-action stack for clamshell packing, and route failures to remote operators at roughly one pilot per 8-10 arms, priced per case.
why_now: Physical-AI models matured in 2025-26, remote-assist tooling and satellite or 5G links are cheap, and enforcement removed the informal labor pool.
revenue_model: Per-case fee with a minimum monthly commitment per station.
non_obvious_insight: Robots run about 20 hours a day at half human speed, and remote humans fix the rare failures. The result is a labor channel that needs neither a visa nor a robot that never fails.
first_30_days: Rent two arms, set up a clamshell-packing station at one packhouse, and hire three remote operators for a paid pilot.

title: A Teaching Hospital Inside a Dead Hospital
one_liner: Lease a wing of a closed hospital and run it as a full-scale simulation hospital that nursing schools rent by the student-day.
customer: Community-college ADN and BSN programs turning away applicants, state workforce boards, and health systems that want a new-grad pipeline.
problem: Nursing schools turned away a record 93,176 qualified applications in 2025 (AACN, May 2026). The binding constraint is clinical placement sites, plus faculty vacancies above 7%. Many state boards allow up to 50% of clinical hours in high-fidelity simulation, but most school sim labs are a few beds in a converted classroom. Medicaid cuts are pushing more rural hospitals to close.
solution: Lease a closed hospital floor that already has medical gas, patient rooms, nurse stations, ICU bays and an OR. Fill it with liquidation beds and mannequins. Staff it with simulation faculty and local standardized patients such as retirees and theater students. Run immersive multi-day, 12-hour shift simulations from admission to discharge, sold per student-day or by semester cohort. Design to NCSBN and INACSL standards and get state board sign-off.
why_now: The record turned-away numbers landed in May 2026. 38 state boards had specific simulation rules by 2021 and more have followed. Rural closures are rising with the 2025 federal Medicaid cuts, so vacant, fully plumbed buildings are appearing cheaply. The $10B/yr Rural Health Transformation funds (FY26-30) create state workforce money to pay for seats.
revenue_model: $150-300 per student-day, or cohort contracts of $40-120k per semester per program. Health-system sponsorship for pipeline seats. Workforce and state grant funding.
non_obvious_insight: Simulation labs fail from unrealistic space and thin faculty, not from a lack of mannequins, and a dead hospital is the only building that already is the environment, priced at less than replacement cost. The buyer is a school with a waitlist, backed by employers and state money that want more graduates.
first_30_days: Pick two states with permissive simulation rules and long nursing waitlists. Call ADN program directors at 10 community colleges and offer a paid 2-day 'shift-in-a-day' pilot. Identify 3 closed hospitals through state health-department lists. Recruit a retired nurse educator as clinical lead, rent mannequins for a pilot, and charge $12-20k per cohort.
